rows.stem: Find the general solution of the differential equation : \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3e^{2x} + 3e^{4x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\)
rows.solution: The right-hand side looks like it needs work, but it collapses to a single exponential, after which the equation is a direct integration. Take \(3e^{2x}\) out of the numerator and clear the negative power in the denominator: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3e^{2x}\left(1 + e^{2x}\right)}{e^x + \dfrac{1}{e^x}} = \dfrac{3e^{2x}\left(1 + e^{2x}\right)}{\dfrac{e^{2x} + 1}{e^x}}\). The factor \(1 + e^{2x}\) now cancels, leaving \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3e^{2x} \times e^x = 3e^{3x}\). Integrating both sides, \(\int dy = \int 3e^{3x}\,dx\), so \(y = 3 \times \dfrac{e^{3x}}{3} + C\), that is \(y = e^{3x} + C\), which is the required general solution.

rows.stem: Find the shortest distance between the following lines : \(\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 7\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k})\) and \(\vec{r} = (-\hat{i} - \hat{j} - \hat{k}) + \mu(7\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + \hat{k})\).
rows.solution: For two skew lines \(\vec{r} = \vec{a_1} + \lambda \vec{b_1}\) and \(\vec{r} = \vec{a_2} + \mu \vec{b_2}\), the shortest distance is \(\text{S.D.} = \left|\dfrac{(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}) \cdot (\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2})}{|\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}|}\right|\). Here \(\vec{a_1} = 3\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}\), \(\vec{b_1} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\), \(\vec{a_2} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} - \hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b_2} = 7\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + \hat{k}\), so \(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = -4\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}\). The cross product is \(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 7 & -6 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-2 + 6) - \hat{j}(1 - 7) + \hat{k}(-6 + 14) = 4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\). Then \((\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}) \cdot (\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}) = -16 - 36 - 64 = -116\) and \(|\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}| = \sqrt{16 + 36 + 64} = \sqrt{116}\). Hence \(\text{S.D.} = \dfrac{|-116|}{\sqrt{116}} = \dfrac{116}{\sqrt{116}} = \sqrt{116} = 2\sqrt{29}\) units.

The limits are symmetric about the origin, so test the parity of the integrand first. Put \(f(x) = \sin |x| + \cos |x|\). Since \(|-x| = |x|\), we get \(f(-x) = \sin |x| + \cos |x| = f(x)\), so \(f\) is an even function and \(I = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \left(\sin |x| + \cos |x|\right) dx\). On \([0, \pi/2]\) we have \(x \ge 0\), so \(|x| = x\) and \(I = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} (\sin x + \cos x)\,dx\). Integrating, \(I = 2\left(\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} + \left[\sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\right) = 2\left((0 + 1) + (1 - 0)\right) = 2(1 + 1) = 4\). Hence the value of the integral is \(4\).

rows.stem: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curves \(y^2 = x\), \(x = \dfrac{1}{4}\), \(y = 0\) and \(x = 1\), using integration.
rows.solution: The curve \(y^2 = x\) is a right-handed parabola with vertex at the origin; the line \(y = 0\) is the \(x\)-axis, and \(x = \dfrac{1}{4}\), \(x = 1\) are two vertical lines. The region asked for is the strip between these two vertical lines, bounded below by the \(x\)-axis and above by the upper branch \(y = \sqrt{x}\) of the parabola. Integrating with respect to \(x\), the required area is \(A = \int_{1/4}^{1} \sqrt{x}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{1/4}^{1}\). Now \(\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{3/2} = \dfrac{1}{8}\), so \(A = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{8}\right) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{7}{8} = \dfrac{7}{12}\). Hence the enclosed area is \(\dfrac{7}{12}\) square units.
